analysis: Correct. Day completes the time expression and by introduces the means of survival.

label: B
text: day by,
analysis: Incorrect. The comma comes after by and improperly separates that preposition from being passed down.

label: C
text: day. By
analysis: Incorrect. By being passed down through private libraries is a fragment when made a separate sentence.

label: D
text: day; by
analysis: Incorrect. A semicolon cannot introduce this nonfinite prepositional phrase as an independent clause.

label: A
text: information, has generated
analysis: Incorrect. Has generated introduces an extra finite verb and the preceding comma also separates it from the subject.

label: B
text: information, generating
analysis: Correct. Generating supplies a participial modifier set off from the main clause by the existing comma pair.

label: C
text: information generated
analysis: Incorrect. Generated would serve as a finite verb taking artworks as its object, leaving the later became uncoordinated.

label: D
text: information generates
analysis: Incorrect. Generates introduces another finite verb before the main verb became, without a conjunction linking them.

label: A
text: protest; a decision that,
analysis: Incorrect. A semicolon before "a decision that" does not fit because the following words do not form an independent clause.

label: B
text: protest a decision that,
analysis: Incorrect. It runs "protest" and "a decision" together without needed punctuation.

label: C
text: protest. A decision that
analysis: Incorrect. "A decision that..." is a sentence fragment.

label: D
text: protest, a decision that,
analysis: Correct. The commas properly set off the appositive and the interrupting phrase.

label: A
text: In this way,
analysis: Correct. It points back to the shared pseudonym as the means of achieving the result.

label: B
text: On the other hand,
analysis: Incorrect. "On the other hand" signals contrast, but the second sentence gives a result.

label: C
text: For instance,
analysis: Incorrect. "For instance" would introduce an example, not an outcome.

label: D
text: Later,
analysis: Incorrect. "Later" suggests chronology rather than method.

label: A
text: Specifically,
analysis: Correct. It signals that the second sentence gives specific details about the first.

label: B
text: Instead,
analysis: Incorrect. "Instead" would signal replacement, but the second sentence elaborates.

label: C
text: All the same,
analysis: Incorrect. "All the same" signals concession, which is not present.

label: D
text: Therefore,
analysis: Incorrect. "Therefore" signals a result, but the second sentence is a specification.

label: A
text: Indeed,
analysis: Correct. It emphasizes and expands on the claim that the pseudonym did more than conceal authorship.

label: B
text: However,
analysis: Incorrect. "However" would signal contrast, but the second sentence supports the first.

label: C
text: In addition,
analysis: Incorrect. "In addition" merely adds another point and is weaker than the confirming explanation needed.

label: D
text: Conversely,
analysis: Incorrect. "Conversely" signals an opposite idea, which is not present.

label: A
text: Humans cannot make ascorbic acid in their bodies, but they can get it from brussels sprouts and grapes.
analysis: Incorrect. It says both foods contain vitamin C but does not compare amounts.

label: B
text: Brussels sprouts contain vitamin C (also known as ascorbic acid); in fact, there is 80 mg of vitamin C in every 100 g of brussels sprouts.
analysis: Incorrect. It gives only the brussels sprouts amount, so it does not fully refute the claim about grapes.

label: C
text: Brussels sprouts contain ascorbic acid (also known as vitamin C), and grapes do too.
analysis: Incorrect. It merely says both contain vitamin C.

label: D
text: With 80 mg of vitamin C per every 100 g, brussels sprouts are actually a better source of vitamin C than grapes, which contain only 10 mg per every 100 g.
analysis: Correct. It uses the comparative numerical evidence needed to refute the claim.

label: A
text: Snow hydrologist Julie Koeberle helps maintain automated snow monitoring stations known as SNOTEL sites.
analysis: Incorrect. It defines SNOTEL sites generally but does not give a specific example.

label: B
text: The SNOTEL site at Castle Creek is one of around 90 automated snow measurement stations in Wyoming.
analysis: Correct. It names Castle Creek as a SNOTEL site and situates it among Wyoming stations.

label: C
text: The data collected by SNOTEL sites can help researchers predict downstream water supplies.
analysis: Incorrect. It describes what SNOTEL data can do, not an example of a site.

label: D
text: Located throughout Wyoming, SNOTEL sites monitor snow conditions.
analysis: Incorrect. It gives general location and function information but no specific site.

label: A
text: Using nautical miles for navigation at sea takes Earth’s curvature into account, whereas measuring distances with latitude and longitude coordinates does not.
analysis: Incorrect. It falsely suggests latitude and longitude do not account for Earth's curvature.

label: B
text: Nautical charts use latitude and longitude to measure long distances; these charts are more accurate than flat maps for measuring distances in seafaring navigation because they account for Earth’s curvature.
analysis: Incorrect. It explains nautical charts but does not connect nautical miles to the coordinate system.

label: C
text: Since they directly correlate to the coordinates on nautical charts, which take into account Earth’s curvature, nautical miles are an efficient way to calculate distances at sea.
analysis: Correct. It links nautical miles to nautical-chart coordinates and Earth's curvature, explaining their navigational use.

label: D
text: Nautical miles are a measure of distance equal to one minute of latitude, which is a feature nautical charts use to calculate distances and positions.
analysis: Incorrect. It defines nautical miles but does not fully explain why that makes them useful in seafaring navigation.

label: A
text: universal
analysis: Correct. "Universal" means found nearly everywhere or shared broadly, matching "almost all mosques include."

label: B
text: elaborate
analysis: Incorrect. "Elaborate" means complex or detailed, but the passage is about how common the feature is, not how ornate it is.

label: C
text: illusory
analysis: Incorrect. "Illusory" means deceptive or unreal, which does not fit a real architectural feature.

label: D
text: idealized
analysis: Incorrect. "Idealized" suggests representing a perfect form, but the sentence is about prevalence.

label: A
text: in Oz, “[Dorothy and her companions] passed through the rest of the forest in safety, and when they came out from its gloom saw before them a steep hill, covered from top to bottom with great pieces of rock.”
analysis: Incorrect. It describes a scene in Oz, not the Kansas house.

label: B
text: in Oz, “Dorothy fell asleep only once, and then she dreamed she was in Kansas, where Aunt Em was telling her how glad she was to have her little girl at home again.”
analysis: Incorrect. It mentions Kansas in a dream but does not describe the house as remote or solitary.

label: C
text: in Kansas, “Dorothy lived in the midst of the great Kansas prairies, with Uncle Henry, who was a farmer, and Aunt Em, who was the farmer’s wife.”
analysis: Incorrect. It identifies Dorothy’s household but does not show isolation.

label: D
text: in Kansas, “When Dorothy stood in the doorway and looked around, she could see nothing but the great gray prairie on every side. Not a tree nor a house broke the broad sweep of flat country.”
analysis: Correct. It directly depicts the house as surrounded by empty prairie with no nearby trees or houses.

label: A
text: the evolutionary benefits of a crablike body form are less certain than many studies of carcinization had previously implied.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not broadly reject the benefits of a crablike body form; it complicates the idea that the crablike form is always optimal.

label: B
text: despite having many living relatives, some decarcinized groups did not benefit from decarcinization.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage says many decarcinized groups have few living relatives, and it does not claim frog crabs failed to benefit from decarcinization.

label: C
text: sideways walking may have been less important to the survival of frog crabs than a protected abdomen and other traits associated with carcinization.
analysis: Incorrect. This focuses on particular traits but does not complete the broader conclusion about ecological conditions.

label: D
text: a crablike body form may not be optimal in all cases, with ecological conditions sometimes favoring the persistence of decarcinization.
analysis: Correct. It draws the supported conclusion that ecological conditions can sometimes favor decarcinized forms.

label: A
text: cause other conservationists to adopt a new methodology for counting populations.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not suggest the study will create a new counting method for other conservationists.

label: B
text: risk making inaccurate conclusions about the effectiveness of different conservation strategies.
analysis: Correct. The counting difficulty directly threatens the accuracy of conclusions about strategy effectiveness.

label: C
text: benefit from including species beyond the northern muriqui.
analysis: Incorrect. The issue is not that the study includes too few species; it is that this species is hard to count.

label: D
text: fail to consider less-well-known conservation approaches for the northern muriqui.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not say the study ignores any conservation approaches.

text: crack, or

label: C
text: crack
analysis: Incorrect. It also omits the needed comma before the main clause.

label: D
text: crack,
analysis: Correct. It keeps "groove or crack" together and adds the required comma after the introductory phrase.

text: is not
analysis: Incorrect. "is" does not agree with the plural subject "languages."

analysis: Correct. "Are not" agrees with the plural subject and fits the present-tense contrast.

label: C

analysis: Incorrect. "Was" is singular and past tense.

label: D
text: has not been
analysis: Incorrect. "Has" is singular and creates an incorrect verb phrase here.

analysis: Incorrect. "Their" is plural and does not agree with the singular North Sea.

label: A
text: these personas include specific details (demographics, browsing habits, etc.) that UX designers draw from actual users.
analysis: Correct. "These personas" is the noun being described as fictional yet realistic.

text: specific details that UX designers draw from actual users (demographics, browsing habits, etc.) are included in these personas.
analysis: Incorrect. It makes "specific details" the subject, but details are not what are fictional yet realistic.

text: UX designers include specific details (demographics, browsing habits, etc.) drawn from actual users in these personas.
analysis: Incorrect. It makes UX designers the subject, creating a misplaced modifier.

label: D
text: actual users are the source of the specific details (demographics, browsing habits, etc.) that UX designers include in these personas.
analysis: Incorrect. It makes actual users the subject, also creating a misplaced modifier.

label: A
text: uncontroversial
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not discuss whether the dates are controversial.

label: B

analysis: Incorrect. The dates still matter; the problem is that they cannot be exact.

text: applicable
analysis: Incorrect. "Applicable" does not express the idea of inexact dating.

label: D
text: approximate
analysis: Correct. "Approximate" means close but not exact, which follows directly from the impossibility of precise dating.

text: usually,
analysis: Incorrect. "Usually" suggests frequency, which is not the relationship between the ideas.

label: B
text: for instance,
analysis: Incorrect. "For instance" introduces an example, but the second clause is a result, not an example.

label: C
text: in any case,
analysis: Incorrect. "In any case" suggests a shift or dismissal, not a cause-and-result relationship.

analysis: Correct. "In doing so" shows that by serving, Johnson earned his place in history.

label: A
text: To take one well-known example,
analysis: Incorrect. Chernow is not an example of the common lack of sources; his case is the opposite.

label: B
text: In accordance with this premise,
analysis: Incorrect. "In accordance with this premise" would suggest agreement with the lack-of-sources idea, but the Hamilton example contrasts with it.

label: C
text: It thus came as no surprise that,
analysis: Incorrect. The abundance of sources is not presented as an unsurprising result of the first sentence.

label: D
text: On the other end of the spectrum,
analysis: Correct. It introduces the opposite situation: a biographer with extensive written sources.

label: A
text: Judeth Insel played on India Arie’s first studio album, Acoustic Soul, which was released one year before her album Voyage to India.
analysis: Incorrect. It discusses albums and dates but does not mention Ricky Quiñones’s different contribution.

label: B
text: Both musicians have played on India Arie albums, but Judeth Insel played viola, whereas Ricky Quiñones played guitar.
analysis: Correct. It states a shared connection to India Arie albums and then emphasizes the difference: viola versus guitar.

label: C
text: Acoustic Soul and Voyage to India, released in 2001 and 2002, respectively, are albums by singer and songwriter India Arie.
analysis: Incorrect. It identifies albums and dates but does not compare the musicians.

label: D
text: Judeth Insel and Ricky Quiñones have both lent their musical talents to albums by India Arie.
analysis: Incorrect. It emphasizes similarity, not difference.

label: A
text: Vaalbara and Euramerica were both supercontinents, single landmasses made up of most or all of Earth’s continents.
analysis: Incorrect. It defines supercontinents but does not emphasize formation order.

label: B
text: The supercontinent Euramerica formed long after the supercontinent Vaalbara.
analysis: Correct. It clearly states the chronological relationship between the two supercontinents.

label: C
text: Forming and breaking apart over hundreds of millions of years, supercontinents are made up of most or all of Earth’s continents.
analysis: Incorrect. It describes the supercontinent cycle generally, not the order of these two examples.

label: D
text: Vaalbara formed about 3.6 billion years ago but eventually broke apart.
analysis: Incorrect. It mentions only Vaalbara and does not compare it with Euramerica.

label: A
text: Grimanesa Amoros often employs LED lights in her work, but the smooth LED domes of Uros Island stand in contrast to the tangled LED tubes of Golden Connection.
analysis: Correct. It directly contrasts the forms/materials of the two works.

label: B
text: Uros Island and Golden Connection are two LED light sculptures by well-known artist Grimanesa Amoros.
analysis: Incorrect. It emphasizes a similarity: both are LED sculptures by Amoros.

label: C
text: In 2011, Grimanesa Amoros debuted Uros Island, a part of her Uros series.
analysis: Incorrect. It discusses only Uros Island and does not compare the works.

label: D
text: Many of Grimanesa Amoros's sculptures, like Uros Island and Golden Connection, incorporate LED lights in the form of domes or tubes.
analysis: Incorrect. It groups the works together rather than clearly emphasizing their difference.

label: A
text: Dichloromethane, a hydrochlorocarbon, is composed of hydrogen, chlorine, and carbon; tetradecafluorohexane, a perfluorocarbon, is composed of fluorine and carbon.
analysis: Correct. It directly contrasts the compounds by class and elemental composition.

label: B
text: Dichloromethane and tetradecafluorohexane are chemical compounds used in cooling technologies; the compounds are known as refrigerants.
analysis: Incorrect. It states what the compounds have in common, not how they differ.

label: C
text: The hydrochlorocarbon dichloromethane and the perfluorocarbon tetradecafluorohexane are both refrigerants that can be used in cooling technologies like air conditioners.
analysis: Incorrect. It names the two categories but mainly emphasizes that both are refrigerants used in cooling.

label: D
text: Tetradecafluorohexane, a refrigerant, can be used in cooling technologies to absorb heat and release cold air.
analysis: Incorrect. It discusses only tetradecafluorohexane.

label: A
text: In 1994, Raj Reddy won the A.M. Turing Award for pioneering the development of large-scale artificial intelligence systems.
analysis: Incorrect. It explains Raj Reddy’s award but not whom the award is named for.

label: B
text: The A.M. Turing Award is given for “major contributions of lasting importance to computing.”
analysis: Incorrect. It explains why the award is given, not its namesake.

label: C
text: The A.M. Turing Award is named for groundbreaking British mathematician Alan Turing.
analysis: Correct. It states that the award is named for Alan Turing.

label: D
text: It was in 1994 that Raj Reddy won the A.M. Turing Award.
analysis: Incorrect. It only states when Raj Reddy won the award.

label: A
text: Discrepancies between
analysis: Correct. "Discrepancies between" means differences or mismatches, which explains why ecologists would question the descriptions.

label: B
text: Proclamations of
analysis: Incorrect. "Proclamations of" would mean announcements, which does not create a logical reason for doubt.

label: C
text: Recurrences of
analysis: Incorrect. "Recurrences of" means repeated instances, not conflict between descriptions and observations.

label: D
text: Affinities between
analysis: Incorrect. "Affinities between" means similarities or connections, the opposite of the mismatch needed here.

label: A
text: To present the narrator's belief that she understands Dot better than Celestine does
analysis: Correct. The passage presents the narrator’s belief that she understands Dot better than Celestine does.

label: B
text: To speculate that when Dot is older, her personality will be like Celestine's
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not predict that Dot will grow up to resemble Celestine.

label: C
text: To discuss what the narrator and Celestine do to amuse Dot
analysis: Incorrect. The focus is not on amusing Dot.

label: D
text: To compare the narrator's physical appearance to the physical appearance of Celestine
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not compare the narrator’s and Celestine’s appearances.

label: A
text: It introduces a certain technique, mentions the hypothesis of a study into an ecological consequence of that technique, and presents evidence in support of that study's hypothesis.
analysis: Incorrect. The study's last sentence is its finding, not a hypothesis followed by separate supporting evidence.

label: B
text: It provides an example of a location that has adopted a particular approach, explains the methodology of a study into an ecological effect of that approach, and describes a finding of that study.
analysis: Correct. Example, methodology, and finding appear in precisely that order.

label: C
text: It makes a claim about the use of a specific strategy, describes field observations of a consequence of that strategy in a particular ecosystem, and makes a supposition based on those observations.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage identifies a formal survey method and reports its conclusion, rather than ending with an unsupported supposition.

label: D
text: It presents a solution to a commonly occurring problem, summarizes the procedures used by a group of researchers studying the environmental impact of that solution, and notes the significance of the researchers' findings.
analysis: Incorrect. The last sentence states what the researchers found; it does not go on to discuss the significance of their finding.

label: A
text: Cryptology is a field that focuses primarily on securely managing data.
analysis: Incorrect. It defines cryptology, but that detail is too narrow to be the main idea.

label: B
text: Women such as Dorothy T. Blum and Maureen Baginski have contributed to the field of cryptology.
analysis: Correct. It captures the passage’s central focus on women’s contributions to cryptology.

label: C
text: Dorothy T. Blum and Maureen Baginski worked together on an important project in the field of cryptology.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage never says Blum and Baginski worked together.

label: D
text: Cryptology should be taught more often in schools to encourage more women to enter the field.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not argue that cryptology should be taught more often in schools.

label: A
text: Those otters whose diet consists mainly of snails will likely exhibit less tooth damage than will those otters that use tools to consume mussels and clams.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage says tool use helps otters avoid tooth damage when processing hard-shelled prey; it does not suggest snail-eating otters have less tooth damage than tool users.

label: B
text: Those otters that do not use tools will likely have more robust health than those otters that do use tools.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage identifies fitness benefits for tool-using otters, not better health for non-tool users.

label: C
text: Those otters that do not use tools will likely need to process larger amounts of prey to meet their energy requirements than will those otters that use tools.
analysis: Correct. It follows from the contrast between energy-poor prey and high-quality prey.

label: D
text: Those otters that consume mussels and clams without the use of tools will likely spend less time foraging than will those otters that use tools to access the same prey resources.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not support a claim about shorter foraging time for otters eating mussels and clams without tools.

label: A
text: dissociate from
analysis: Dissociate from 表示与……分离；将物品与文化变化分开，违背其作为文化证据的作用。

label: B
text: collude with
analysis: Collude with 表示与人秘密勾结，既不适用于物品与抽象变化的关系，也与史料价值无关。

label: C
text: compensate for
analysis: Compensate for 表示弥补某种损失或不足；文中不是要弥补 shifts，而是要显示这些变化。

label: D
text: attest to
analysis: Attest to 表示证明或为……提供证据，与前文 evidence 及后面的文化变化一一衔接。

label: A
text: Samples of animal remains collected at Calusa sites reflect a greater diversity of marine species, particularly among sea snails, within the perimeter of watercourts than in locations known to have been devoted to the preparation and consumption of food.
analysis: Incorrect. Greater diversity of marine remains within watercourts could support, not weaken, the idea that watercourts fostered sea snails.

label: B
text: Historical population-size estimates suggest that the sea snails and fish most common in the Calusa diet were plentiful in open coastal waters when the watercourts were constructed but decreased in abundance in the years immediately after construction.
analysis: Incorrect. This explains why managed food sources may have been useful but does not directly undermine conch cultivation.

label: C
text: Radar surveys of Calusa sites reveal watercourt dimensions suitable for sustaining fish of many local species but not conducive for maintaining the shallow environments with ample seagrasses that allow sea snails to thrive.
analysis: Correct. It directly challenges whether the watercourts could sustain conditions needed for conch.

label: D
text: Sediment layers excavated from Calusa watercourt sites contain heterogeneous mixtures of scales from multiple species of fish and fragments of shells from various types of sea snails, but conch shells do not constitute the majority of the mixture in most of those layers.
analysis: Incorrect. It notes mixed remains and no concentration of conch, but choice C more directly attacks the environmental feasibility of Schober’s hypothesis.

label: A
text: are helpful starting points for studying computer games as art, even though these frameworks are overly simplistic.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not say Nguyen treats those frameworks as helpful starting points; it says they fail to capture a central aspect.

label: B
text: are useful for analyzing the narrative aspects of computer games, even if neither attempts to address player agency.
analysis: Incorrect. Although narrative is mentioned, the conclusion concerns the inadequacy of frameworks that miss player agency, not their usefulness for narrative analysis.

label: C
text: overstate the influence of fiction and cinema on the narrative elements of computer games.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not claim fiction and cinema influence computer-game narratives too much.

label: D
text: subsume computer games under other categories of media that do not address a feature of games that is integral to player enjoyment.
analysis: Correct. It captures the idea that the frameworks classify games under other media while missing player agency.

label: A
text: researchers ought to account for the possibility that because MPB have the capacity to compensate for reduced sunlight availability, benthic chlorophyll concentrations may not always be a reliable indicator of MPB biomass.
analysis: Correct. It follows from the warning that MPB can compensate for low light by producing more chlorophyll.

label: B
text: although their finding was inconsistent with that of García-Robledo and Corzo, this discrepancy was not attributable to the ability of MPB to accelerate chlorophyll production to mitigate the negative impact of macroalgal accumulations.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage says the compensation possibility helps explain why chlorophyll may not show a negative correlation, not that it is irrelevant.

label: C
text: although elevated levels of macroalgae do not always correspond to increased levels of benthic chlorophyll, there is likely a larger trend in MPB biomass that is related to macroalgal presence but unrelated to light conditions.
analysis: Incorrect. It speculates about a larger trend unrelated to sunlight, which is not supported.

label: D
text: the effect of macroalgal concentrations on MPB abundance that García-Robledo and Corzo reported was not observed in Curlew Bay and other Virginia sites because low-light conditions likely are not generalizable across the sites in the studies.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not conclude that low-light effects are not generalizable; it questions chlorophyll concentration as a proxy.

label: A
text: a person who perceives certain odors as pleasant will likely perceive the odors as roughly equal in pleasantness.
analysis: Incorrect. The study compares different odors across people, not whether one person rates pleasant odors as equally pleasant.

label: B
text: culture significantly influences whether a person perceives an odor as pleasant or unpleasant.
analysis: Correct. Similar ratings across cultures weaken the claim that culture significantly shapes odor pleasantness.

label: C
text: personal taste has little influence on whether odors are perceived as pleasant or unpleasant.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not show that personal taste has little influence; it focuses on culture.

label: D
text: people agree in their perception of odors as pleasant or unpleasant regardless of where they live.
analysis: Incorrect. This restates the study’s finding rather than the idea that the finding undermines.

label: A
text: levels of dissolved organic carbon and mercury are both much higher in bodies of fresh water impacted by wastewater than they are in bodies of fresh water disturbed by urban development.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not compare absolute levels of carbon and mercury in wastewater versus urban-development waters.

label: B
text: Guédron, Tisserand, and colleagues' study used different methods to measure the concentration of mercury in fresh water than Tjerngren and colleagues' study did.
analysis: Incorrect. Different measurement methods are not discussed.

label: C
text: the effects of wastewater on the association between levels of dissolved organic carbon and mercury should not be taken as indicative of the effects of every type of human disturbance.
analysis: Correct. The urban-development study shows that wastewater effects are not representative of all human disturbances.

label: D
text: disturbances linked to wastewater affect significantly more bodies of fresh water than disturbances linked to urban development do.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not compare how widespread wastewater and urban-development disturbances are.

text: information, has generated
analysis: Incorrect. Has generated adds an uncoordinated finite verb and is also separated from its subject by a comma.

text: information generates
analysis: Incorrect. Generates introduces an extra finite predicate before became.

label: C
text: information, generating
analysis: Correct. Generating forms a supplementary participial phrase describing the documentation.

label: D
text: information generated
analysis: Incorrect. Generated would be a finite verb taking artworks as its object, leaving the later became without coordination.

text: protest a decision that,
analysis: Incorrect. It runs "protest" and "a decision" together without needed punctuation.

label: B
text: protest. A decision that
analysis: Incorrect. A period makes "A decision that..." a fragment.

label: C
text: protest; a decision that,
analysis: Incorrect. The semicolon incorrectly separates a noun phrase from the sentence.

label: D
text: protest, a decision that,
analysis: Correct. The commas correctly introduce the appositive and set off the interrupting phrase.

label: A
text: In this way,
analysis: Correct. It shows that publishing under the shared name enabled the joint creative expression described next.

label: B
text: For instance,
analysis: Incorrect. "For instance" would introduce an example, but the second sentence states a result.

label: C
text: Later,
analysis: Incorrect. "Later" suggests a time sequence, not a method-result relationship.

label: A
text: McAllister et al. suggest that spike waves can form when traveling waves propagating in opposing directions intersect and that spike waves tend to be higher than traveling waves.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage says spike waves can exceed a constraint on traveling-wave height, not that they generally tend to be higher than traveling waves.

label: B
text: The process of breaking limits the height of traveling waves, but the study by McAllister et al. suggests that spike waves can exceed those limits if their height-to-length ratio reaches a critical threshold.
analysis: Incorrect. It falsely applies the height-to-length threshold condition to spike waves; the passage says other factors mediate spike-wave breaking.

label: C
text: The study by McAllister et al. suggests that when traveling waves intersect in specific ways, the resulting wave may be higher than would be expected based on the properties of traveling waves.
analysis: Correct. It captures the formation of spike waves and the finding that they can exceed expectations based on traveling-wave constraints.

label: D
text: Previous studies have suggested that steepness mediates breaking in traveling waves, but the study by McAllister et al. shows that jet stability and cavity shape may also influence breaking in such waves.
analysis: Incorrect. Jet stability and cavity shape are factors for spike-wave breaking, not for traveling-wave breaking.

label: A
text: "Stevens's ambassadorial sandpaintings are best understood not as self-contained objects but as reminders of the public creations of the sandpaintings, during which Stevens conducted appropriate ikaah rituals and encouraged viewers to closely track his movements and subtle shifts in the sand throughout the process."
analysis: Correct. It connects the preserved works to the dynamic public practice of creating ikaah.

label: B
text: "While Stevens's ambassadorial sandpaintings are undoubtedly educational for audiences that have little exposure to Diné culture, they should not be confused with authentic ikaah, which cannot be extricated from a practice that is intentionally and necessarily transitory nor condensed into a single persistent object."
analysis: Incorrect. It says the preserved works should not be confused with authentic ikaah, which undercuts rather than supports the passage's claim.

label: C
text: "The most compelling way to reconcile the apparent tension between the temporary and performative nature of ikaah and the persistent and static nature of Stevens's ambassadorial sandpaintings is to recognize that Stevens was an ambassador not only of Diné culture but of a US art culture that tended to value permanent works over ephemeral ones."
analysis: Incorrect. It shifts the explanation to US art culture's preference for permanence, not Stevens's effort to convey ikaah's dynamic characteristics.

label: D
text: "It is important to recall Stevens's own actions as a gift-giver—a temporary and performative role—of the sandpaintings, for by taking those actions, Stevens publicly enacted the transmission of knowledge of both traditional ikaah practices and cutting-edge chemistry (in the form of the preservative additives), a hybrid that reflects the dynamism of Diné culture."
analysis: Incorrect. It emphasizes gift-giving and chemistry, but it does not as directly support the claim about conveying the sandpainting practice itself.

label: A
text: Half of the spiders that first looked at a termite wearing a black-and-white striped cape attacked a termite wearing a solid white cape, and the other half of those spiders were just as likely to attack a termite wearing a black-and-white striped cape as they were to attack a termite wearing a solid black cape.
analysis: Incorrect. It accurately describes one row but emphasizes a split within the striped-first row rather than the broad deterrence pattern.

label: B
text: For each type of cape, a majority of the spiders that first looked at a termite wearing that type of cape attacked a termite wearing that same type of cape.
analysis: Incorrect. It is false; for the striped-first row, only 25% attacked striped capes.

label: C
text: Regardless of the type of cape worn by termites the spiders first looked at, the large majority of spider attacks were on termites wearing solid-color capes.
analysis: Correct. It captures the consistent full-table pattern supporting the researchers' conclusion.

label: D
text: None of the spiders that first looked at a termite wearing a solid white cape attacked a termite wearing a black-and-white striped cape.
analysis: Incorrect. It is true for one row, but it is narrower than the best table-wide evidence.

analysis: Correct. It directly challenges the expected opposite-direction pattern of a linear time axis.

analysis: Incorrect. The text does not say historians should ignore concerns about embellishment.

label: B
text: Historians' fidelity to the truth often results in work that is less engaging than it could be.
analysis: Correct. It summarizes the tension between fidelity to truth and engaging presentation.

label: C
text: Historians do not agree among themselves about the best methods of recording history.
analysis: Incorrect. The text does not describe disagreement among historians.

label: D
text: Maps are more practical to own than paintings.
analysis: Incorrect. The map/painting comparison is metaphorical, not about ownership or practicality.

label: A
text: the Ardagh Hoard and Balline Hoard were both found before 2000.
analysis: Correct. Both listed discovery years are before 2000.

label: B
text: Balline Hoard and Carrick-on-Suir Hoard were both discovered in the 1900s.
analysis: Incorrect. Carrick-on-Suir was discovered in 2013, not the 1900s.

label: C
text: the Balline Hoard was found in 1868.
analysis: Incorrect. Balline was found in 1940; Ardagh was found in 1868.

label: D
text: the Ardagh Hoard, Balline Hoard, and Carrick-on-Suir Hoard have all been found since 1868.
analysis: Incorrect. Carrick-on-Suir was found after 1868, but the choice does not support the 'found earlier' point as clearly as A and includes a twenty-first-century example.

label: A
text: accommodation/food services but below both health care and retail.
analysis: It correctly places accommodation/food services below tribal activity and both retail and health care above it.

label: B
text: health care, retail, and accommodation/food services.
analysis: Retail and health care exceed tribal activity, so tribal activity cannot rank above all three.

label: C
text: accommodation/food services and nearly equal to health care and retail.
analysis: The retail and health-care totals are substantially larger, not nearly equal to tribal activity.

label: D
text: both accommodation/food services and retail but below health care.
analysis: Tribal activity does not exceed retail's$10.7billion total.

label: A
text: iris color in domestic dogs may be an adaptation to elicit positive responses from humans, as participants responded more negatively to images of dogs whose iris colors can make pupils appear large than they did to images of dogs without such iris colors.
analysis: Incorrect. It says participants responded more negatively to the iris colors associated with larger-looking pupils, which reverses the data.

label: B
text: humans may not be as sensitive to pupil size in dogs as they are to pupil size in other people, as participants' responses to the images show no relationship to differences in the shade of dogs' irises that could affect how large the dogs' pupils appear to be.
analysis: Incorrect. The table does show a relationship between iris shade and more positive ratings.

label: C
text: humans' responses to pupil size in other people may extend to dogs, as participants responded more positively to images of dogs whose iris colors were likely to make their pupils appear large than they did to images of dogs whose iris colors were unlikely to have that effect.
analysis: Correct. Dark-iris images received higher positive ratings, supporting the idea that larger-looking pupils elicit positive responses.

label: D
text: differences in dogs' pupil size may elicit a stronger response in humans than differences in people's pupil size do, as participants' responses to images when dogs' pupils were actually large were indistinguishable from participants' responses when dogs' pupils only appeared to be large.
analysis: Incorrect. The study concerns iris color and apparent pupil size, not directly measured differences in actual pupil size.

label: A
text: Even though overall usage of the nesting boxes by wasps and birds was high throughout the study, 24% of the manipulated boxes remained vacant each spring, while less than 4% of the unmanipulated nesting boxes remained vacant.
analysis: Incorrect. Vacancy rates do not directly show competition or bird advantage.

label: B
text: Nest initiation by either birds or wasps but not both was observed in more than 90% of the unmanipulated boxes, but nest initiation by wasps was observed in less than 50% of the manipulated boxes.
analysis: Incorrect. It suggests non-co-occupancy but does not clearly show a bird advantage, and its manipulated-box detail is less direct.

label: C
text: Wasps initiated nesting in manipulated boxes much more often than in unmanipulated boxes, and 80% of initial co-occupations of unmanipulated boxes resulted in abandonment by wasps but not by birds.
analysis: Correct. It supports both competition for nest boxes and birds' advantage over wasps.

label: D
text: Although only 15 instances of co-occupation of unmanipulated boxes by wasps and birds were observed over the course of the study, in a majority of those instances, wasps were already occupying the boxes when birds initiated nesting in them.
analysis: Incorrect. It describes some co-occupations but does not show birds consistently outcompeting wasps as directly as C.

label: A
text: Although the site appears to have been a tropical deltaic forest during the Devonian period, fossil evidence suggests that Eospermatopteris was present at that time.
analysis: Incorrect. Eospermatopteris in a tropical deltaic forest fits the partition hypothesis.

label: B
text: The site appears to have been a tropical deltaic forest early in the Devonian period but transitioned to an arid floodplain forest after the end of the Devonian period.
analysis: Incorrect. A transition after the Devonian period does not contradict the Devonian-period partition hypothesis.

label: C
text: The site appears to have been an arid floodplain forest during the Devonian period and contains fossil evidence of contemporaneous Eospermatopteris and Archaeopteris.
analysis: Correct. It places both plant types together in one Devonian biome, directly challenging the partition hypothesis.

label: D
text: Fossil evidence from the site suggests that several forest plant species other than Eospermatopteris and Archaeopteris lived there during the Devonian period.
analysis: Incorrect. Additional species do not directly undermine the claimed partition between the two named plant-biome associations.

label: A
text: The study by Hikwama had a lower traceability rating than the study by Townsend and colleagues did.
analysis: Incorrect. Traceability concerns clarity of procedures, not specificity of reported data.

label: B
text: The study by Hikwama had a lower detail rating than the study by Townsend and colleagues did.
analysis: Correct. A lower detail rating directly challenges the claim that Hikwama's data were more specific.

label: C
text: The study by Hikwama had a high detail rating and a high traceability rating.
analysis: Incorrect. A high detail rating would support, not challenge, the conclusion.

label: D
text: The study by Townsend and colleagues had a low detail rating and a low traceability rating.
analysis: Incorrect. Low ratings for Townsend would not challenge the claim that Hikwama was more specific.

label: A
text: outdated
analysis: Incorrect. "Outdated" means no longer current or useful. The text evaluates the range of Lecuona's music, not whether it has become obsolete.

label: B
text: varied
analysis: Correct. "Varied" describes the diversity demonstrated by orchestral pieces, operas, and film scores.

label: C
text: forgotten
analysis: Incorrect. "Forgotten" would claim that people no longer remember the music. Nothing in the passage addresses its later popularity or survival.

label: D
text: lonely
analysis: Incorrect. "Lonely" describes isolation or lack of companionship, not the range of genres within a composer's output.

label: A
text: She was gaining an unfair advantage over other contestants in the talent show.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage describes her practice habits, not an advantage she gained over other talent-show contestants.

label: B
text: She was lying to herself about her musical ability.
analysis: Incorrect. She admits that she dawdles and does not listen closely; she does not describe convincing herself that she has greater musical ability.

label: C
text: She was deceiving her piano teacher.
analysis: Incorrect. No teacher's presence, awareness, or deception is described. This adds a target of dishonesty that the text does not identify.

label: D
text: she was violating an expectation about how to perform the piece.
analysis: Correct. Looking at the notes instead of relying on memory violates the explicitly stated expectation for playing the piece.

label: A
text: contributions
analysis: Correct. "Contributions" accurately refers to the excerpts supplied by volunteers for the dictionary's work.

label: B
text: resolutions
analysis: Incorrect. "Resolutions" would mean decisions or solutions. The volunteers supply documentary materials rather than settle a question by making a resolution.

label: C
text: justifications
analysis: Incorrect. "Justifications" are reasons offered to defend a claim or action. The passage instead identifies excerpts submitted as research evidence.

label: D
text: negotiations
analysis: Incorrect. "Negotiations" are discussions aimed at reaching an agreement. No bargaining or agreement-seeking is described.

label: A
text: intercede in
analysis: Incorrect. "Intercede in" means intervene in a dispute or situation. The passage describes firms locating near one another, not mediating a conflict.

label: B
text: concur with
analysis: Incorrect. "Concur with" means agree with. An area is not an opinion with which the firms can agree.

label: C
text: appeal to
analysis: Incorrect. "Appeal to" means attract or request something from someone. It does not express the firms' geographic concentration.

label: D
text: amass in
analysis: Correct. "Amass in" describes many related firms gathering in one area, matching the passage's own word "cluster."

label: A
text: It contrasts great-uncle Richard's wary first impressions of Adam with his ultimate affection toward him.
analysis: Incorrect. Richard is not initially wary: the meeting is described as auspicious from the beginning.

label: B
text: It showcases how Adam's flexibility and consideration strengthen his relationship with his great-uncle Richard.
analysis: Correct. Adam's willingness to follow Richard's preferences leads directly to Richard's affection and their growing friendship.

label: C
text: It states the reasons why Adam and his great-uncle Richard decide to sleep on the ship rather than finding lodging on land.
analysis: Incorrect. The overnight invitation helps demonstrate Adam's consideration; the passage does not compare shipboard lodging with lodging on land.

label: D
text: It describes why Adam and his great-uncle Richard are excited for their upcoming journey on the ship.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not establish a shared upcoming journey on the ship. Richard's interest in the vessel prompts an invitation to stay aboard.

label: A
text: It introduces the topic of a scientific study, describes the study's importance, and then presents the study's results.
analysis: Incorrect. The text opens with an approach to research rather than the butterfly study's topic, and it does not present the study's results.

label: B
text: It identifies a particular approach to research, lists some benefits of that approach, and then mentions a study in which that approach was used.
analysis: Correct. This reproduces the sequence of definition, benefits, and a concrete example of use.

label: C
text: It argues for a new approach to scientific research, comments on the public's opinion about the approach, and then describes how that approach was applied in a certain study.
analysis: Incorrect. No public opinion is reported, and the approach is not described as newly developed.

label: D
text: It describes the development of a type of scientific collaboration, shows how that type of collaboration has been used in a particular field of study, and then suggests future collaborative projects.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not recount how the collaboration developed over time or propose future projects.

label: A
text: LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes is visited by more people.
analysis: Incorrect. There are no visitor totals for either institution, so their attendance cannot be compared.

label: B
text: LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes has more objects in its collection.
analysis: Incorrect. Only the Museo's collection size is given. LA Plaza's number of objects is not stated.

label: C
text: LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes is housed in a larger building.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage provides no building-size information.

label: D
text: LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes opened more recently.
analysis: Correct. 2011 is later than 1991, establishing that LA Plaza opened more recently.

label: A
text: "We would all go in company to see if the flowers we were named for were yet in bloom, for almost all the girls are named for flowers."
analysis: Incorrect. Naming girls for flowers is a custom, but the quotation does not directly address the reader.

label: B
text: "Nothing happened during the day, and after awhile mother told us not to say a word about why we left, for grandpa might get mad with us."
analysis: Incorrect. The instruction to remain silent about leaving does not directly address the reader or explain a community custom.

label: C
text: "Now, my dear reader, there is no word so endearing as the word father, and that is why [my people] call all good people father or mother."
analysis: Correct. "My dear reader" supplies direct address, and "that is why" introduces the explanation for calling good people father or mother.

label: D
text: "But how can I describe the scene that followed? Some of you, dear readers, can imagine."
analysis: Incorrect. "Dear readers" supplies direct address, but the quotation concerns imagining a scene rather than explaining a custom.

label: A
text: inform
analysis: Correct. "Museums inform visitors" supplies a complete subject–verb–object structure with plural agreement.

label: B
text: informing
analysis: Incorrect. "Informing" is a participle; without an auxiliary such as are, it leaves the sentence without a finite verb.

label: C
text: to inform
analysis: Incorrect. "To inform" is an infinitive and does not function as the sentence's main verb here.

label: D
text: having informed
analysis: Incorrect. "Having informed" is a participial phrase and likewise leaves the clause without a finite main verb.

label: A
text: is completing
analysis: Incorrect. "Is completing" describes an action in progress now, conflicting with "nearly 150 years ago."

label: B
text: will complete
analysis: Incorrect. "Will complete" places the action in the future, contrary to the explicit past time.

label: C
text: completed
analysis: Correct. "Completed" locates the finished drawing at the stated past time.

label: D
text: has been completing
analysis: Incorrect. "Has been completing" suggests ongoing activity extending toward the present, not a finished event nearly 150 years ago.

label: A
text: phenomenon in
analysis: Incorrect. Without a clause boundary, "phenomenon in 2022, the ... duo ... defeated" runs two independent clauses together.

label: B
text: phenomenon and in
analysis: Incorrect. And can coordinate independent clauses, but this version omits the comma required before that conjunction.

label: C
text: phenomenon. In
analysis: Correct. The period ends the first clause, and capitalized In begins a complete second sentence.

label: D
text: phenomenon, in
analysis: Incorrect. A comma alone cannot join the two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

label: A
text: Nation and in
analysis: Incorrect. And introduces a second independent clause but lacks the preceding comma needed for that coordination.

label: B
text: Nation in
analysis: Incorrect. With no punctuation before in, the two independent clauses are run together.

label: C
text: Nation, in
analysis: Incorrect. A comma before in is insufficient to separate the complete clauses, producing a comma splice.

label: D
text: Nation. In
analysis: Correct. A period properly separates the identification of the chapter from the statement of its name in another language.

label: A
text: century; revealing
analysis: Incorrect. A semicolon must separate independent clauses; "revealing how..." is a participial phrase rather than an independent clause.

label: B
text: century, revealing
analysis: Correct. The comma appropriately sets off the supplementary explanation beginning with revealing.

label: C
text: century. Revealing
analysis: Incorrect. After the period, "Revealing how..." has no finite main verb and is a sentence fragment.

label: D
text: century revealing
analysis: Incorrect. Omitting the comma fails to mark the supplementary phrase that follows the complete exploration statement.

label: A
text: Therefore,
analysis: Incorrect. "Therefore" would present the ranks as a consequence of the earlier comparison, rather than as the underlying details of it.

label: B
text: Specifically,
analysis: Correct. "Specifically" signals that third and fifteenth make the earlier statement more precise.

label: C
text: On the other hand,
analysis: Incorrect. "On the other hand" introduces a contrast, but the exact ranks support the preceding claim.

label: D
text: Later,
analysis: Incorrect. "Later" suggests a subsequent event or time; the passage reports details from the same compiled rankings.

label: A
text: still,
analysis: Correct. "Still" introduces the unexpected accuracy achieved despite the crude technique.

label: B
text: Fittingly.
analysis: Incorrect. "Fittingly" would suggest that accuracy was an appropriate or expected result, weakening the contrast emphasized by "apparently crude."

label: C
text: Similarly,
analysis: Incorrect. "Similarly" requires a comparable method or result before it; the first sentence instead introduces the crude technique.

label: D
text: In other words,
analysis: Incorrect. "In other words" would restate the first sentence, but the second evaluates the method's accuracy using new information.

label: A
text: fittingly,
analysis: Incorrect. "Fittingly" would treat the intact ring as consistent with expectations, but its location makes it unexpected.

label: B
text: for example,
analysis: Incorrect. "For example" would introduce a case illustrating the rule. This case contradicts the stated prediction for an outside ring.

label: C
text: likewise,
analysis: Incorrect. "Likewise" signals similarity, whereas the observed intact ring differs from the expected outcome.

label: D
text: though,
analysis: Correct. "Though" appropriately introduces an observation at odds with the expectation of accretion outside the limit.

label: A
text: The sound of black-tailed gulls was included on a list of 100 soundscapes.
analysis: Incorrect. This identifies the sound's inclusion on a list but does not tell the audience where to hear it.

label: B
text: The soundscape was selected by the Japanese Ministry of the Environment for its cultural significance to Japan.
analysis: Incorrect. This explains who selected the soundscape and why, rather than where it is located.

label: C
text: The soundscape included the sounds heard in a specific place.
analysis: Incorrect. This restates what a soundscape is without naming a specific place.

label: D
text: The sound of black-tailed gulls at Hachinohe Port can be heard in Aomori Prefecture on northern Honshu Island, Japan.
analysis: Correct. This supplies a particular sound and a precise geographic location, fulfilling the where-focused goal.

label: A
text: Most plant species found in Oahu, Hawaii, like Trema orientalis, are non- native.
analysis: Incorrect. This states that Trema orientalis is non-native but never contrasts it with Ilex anomala.

label: B
text: A 2019 study catalogued plant seeds found in bird fecal samples in Oahu, Hawaii, to determine what role non-native birds play in seed dispersal.
analysis: Incorrect. This describes the study's method and purpose without comparing the two plants.

label: C
text: Though Ilex anomala and Trema orientalis can both be found in Oahu, Hawaii, only the former plant is native.
analysis: Correct. This identifies the shared location and then explicitly distinguishes the native plant from the non-native one.

label: D
text: Seeds from Ilex anomala and Trema orientalis plants were found in the fecal samples of non-native Hawaiian birds, according to a 2019 study.
analysis: Incorrect. This emphasizes a similarity: seeds of both plants were found in the birds' samples.

label: A
text: retroactively
analysis: Incorrect. "Retroactively" concerns applying something to an earlier time, not sharing recognition among several people.

label: B
text: ceremoniously
analysis: Incorrect. "Ceremoniously" concerns formal or elaborate presentation. It does not distinguish multiple recipients from a single recipient.

label: C
text: jointly
analysis: Correct. "Jointly" expresses that the award is given to the credited individuals together.

label: D
text: reluctantly
analysis: Incorrect. "Reluctantly" would imply unwillingness, but the committee is described as wanting to reward the shared work.

label: A
text: sustainable
analysis: Incorrect. "Sustainable" means capable of being maintained over time. The explanation concerns changing physical form, not long-term viability.

label: B
text: unrivaled
analysis: Incorrect. "Unrivaled" means unmatched in quality or extent. No comparison establishing superiority appears.

label: C
text: immutable
analysis: Incorrect. "Immutable" means unchanging, directly contradicting the description of constant evolution.

label: D
text: dynamic
analysis: Correct. "Dynamic" captures the continual change in the delta's channels and strips of land.

label: A
text: tranquil
analysis: Incorrect. "Tranquil" means calm or peaceful, which does not specifically account for an objective, unsentimental perspective.

label: B
text: peculiar
analysis: Incorrect. "Peculiar" means unusual. It offers no reason that Whistler would anticipate the apparent objectivity of Evans's work.

label: C
text: nostalgic
analysis: Incorrect. "Nostalgic" implies sentimental longing for the past, conflicting with the contrast against sentimental contemporaries.

label: D
text: dispassionate
analysis: Correct. "Dispassionate" expresses the emotionally detached observation that connects Whistler with the later photographs.

label: A
text: It relates how Mr. Ely had initially earned the respect of his colleagues and then recounts the circumstances under which their views of him began to change.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not recount a change from respect to disapproval; the favorable views remain in place.

label: B
text: It implies that Mr. Ely's neighbors are more naïve in their estimation of him than people in London are and then explains why his neighbors have been so easily misled.
analysis: Incorrect. It speculates about Ely's impact in London but gives no actual Londoners' assessment to compare with his neighbors' views.

label: C
text: It presents the favorable opinion of Mr. Ely that other people hold and then describes the behaviors of Mr. Ely that enable him to maintain that favorable opinion.
analysis: Correct. This correctly identifies the sequence from favorable opinions to the careful behaviors that maintain them.

label: D
text: It highlights the disparity between Mr. Ely's public and private behavior and then conveys why he labors to obscure his true self from other people.
analysis: Incorrect. The text does not present contrasting private behavior or explain a motive for concealing a separate true self.

label: A
text: It describes how an algorithm can predict the success of certain businesses, discusses an example of a use of that algorithm, and suggests potential uses of the algorithm in other fields.
analysis: Incorrect. The model predicts a neighborhood's business mix, not whether individual businesses will succeed, and no application in another field is suggested.

label: B
text: It explains why urban planners are interested in understanding the locations of certain businesses, details a study that has addressed this question, and identifies one key finding.
analysis: Incorrect. The opening does not explain urban planners' interests, and the final sentence proposes an application rather than a key finding.

label: C
text: It summarizes trends in recent urban development, describes a potential problem for urban planners, and suggests a computational tool that can be used to solve that problem.
analysis: Incorrect. No recent urban-development trends are summarized; the passage begins directly with the research model.

label: D
text: It introduces a research team's study of urban neighborhoods, describes an aspect of the study's methodology, and suggests a potential application of the team's research.
analysis: Correct. This matches the progression from research introduction to methodology to prospective application.

label: A
text: By arguing that K2-18 b and other hycean candidates are unlikely to support life because these planets are located too far from the stars they orbit
analysis: Incorrect. This reverses the distance problem. Moving the inner boundary outward makes K2-18 b too close to its star, rather than too far away.

label: B
text: By maintaining that Madhusudhan et al. relied on a model whose estimates of surface temperatures on hycean candidates are likely too high
analysis: Incorrect. Tsai's argument implies that earlier estimates understated the heating problem, not that they estimated temperatures too high.

label: C
text: By stating that the chemical composition of the atmosphere of the hycean candidate Madhusudhan et al. identified suggests that this planet's surface is unlikely to harbor liquid water
analysis: Correct. This correctly ties atmospheric composition to an unfavorable prospect for surface liquid water.

label: D
text: By observing that unlike the hycean candidate Madhusudhan et al. discovered, most other types of planets with hydrogen-rich atmospheres are likely located within the Hz
analysis: Incorrect. Neither text compares the locations of most other hydrogen-atmosphere planet types with that of K2-18 b.

label: A
text: Although Ngūgī insisted on publishing his first works in Gīkūyū, they have since been translated into many other languages.
analysis: Incorrect. This incorrectly says his first works were in Gikuyu; the passage states that he had already published four novels in English.

label: B
text: Although Ngũgi's decision to write in Gîkûyû was met with some skepticism, it didn't prevent him from achieving literary success.
analysis: Correct. This captures the warnings about his decision and the literary success he subsequently achieved.

label: C
text: The reaction to Ngûgī's rejection of English illustrates that some literary experts believe that fame is most easily gained by writing in a widely understood language, such as Gīkūyū.
analysis: Incorrect. This incorrectly treats Gikuyu as the widely understood alternative. The critics identified Kiswahili as more widely spoken.

label: D
text: In the 1970s, Ngûgi became convinced that literature ought to be written in authors' native languages, and he proceeded to publish many works in Gikūyū.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage does not attribute to him a general belief that all authors ought to use their native languages, and this choice omits the skepticism–success contrast.

label: A
text: The study's findings suggest that an increase in the number of amenities near city parks would likely increase park use in Quito but not in Buenos Aires.
analysis: Incorrect. This predicts the effects of adding amenities in each city, but the survey comparison establishes no such intervention effect.

label: B
text: Although the study found that a greater proportion of residents use parks in Quito than in Buenos Aires, that difference isn't due to greater access to amenities near parks in Quito.
analysis: Correct. This accurately combines the higher reported park use in Quito with the rejected explanation based on greater nearby-amenity access.

label: C
text: Even though the study found that parks in Buenos Aires are more likely to be close to other amenities than parks in Quito are, Quito has more amenities overall than Buenos Aires does.
analysis: Incorrect. This adds a claim that Quito has more amenities overall, which the passage never makes.

label: D
text: The study's finding that a greater proportion of residents use parks in Quito than in Buenos Aires is partly due to the greater prevalence of parks in Quito.
analysis: Incorrect. The passage provides no comparison of park prevalence and does not identify more parks as a cause of the usage difference.

label: A
text: The high conductivity of the CFRP is what makes the energy output from a piezoelectric harvester sufficient for wireless communication devices.
analysis: Incorrect. This concerns sufficient output and attributes it to conductivity, but it does not explain why the output must remain steady.

label: B
text: The CFRP electrode is incompatible with most wireless communication devices.
analysis: Incorrect. Incompatibility would limit the usefulness of the CFRP device rather than support the claim that steady supply is required.

label: C
text: Intermittent or unpredictable electrical supply undermines the efficacy of wireless communication devices.
analysis: Correct. This directly explains why intermittent supply is inadequate and continuous, predictable energy is necessary.

label: D
text: The near-constant kinetic vibration of a spacecraft makes it possible to power its wireless communication devices using only non-CFRP piezoelectric harvesters.
analysis: Incorrect. This describes a possible alternative energy arrangement; it does not establish that steadiness is required for wireless devices to work.

label: A
text: sílver nanoparticles may increase the metabolic processes of the bacteria, thereby increasing the number of free electrons available to transfer to the electrode.
analysis: Incorrect. This shifts the mechanism to increased bacterial metabolism. The stated evidence concerns silver's conductivity, not its effect on producing electrons.

label: B
text: as the density of the biofilm increases, the series of redox reactions may accelerate independent of the presence of the silver nanoparticles.
analysis: Incorrect. This invokes increasing biofilm density and an effect independent of silver, neither of which explains the reported silver intervention.

label: C
text: silver nanoparticles may allow electrons to bypass the series of redox reactions and transfer directly to the electrode.
analysis: Correct. This connects silver's conductivity with a direct route that avoids the inefficient transfer sequence.

label: D
text: electrons may be conducted directly to the electrode before the silver nanoparticles catalyze the redox reactions.
analysis: Incorrect. This adds an unsupported catalytic role and sequence for silver rather than clearly explaining how conductivity bypasses the bottleneck.

label: A
text: memory and
analysis: And alone omits the comma required at this independent-clause boundary.

label: B
text: memory.
analysis: The period would require capital She and does not match the displayed continuation.

label: C
text: memory, and
analysis: Memory completes the list; comma + and joins the two clauses.

label: D
text: memory
analysis: No separator or conjunction would produce a run-on.

label: A
text: song:
analysis: A colon cannot separate the noun from the identifying title here.

label: B
text: song;
analysis: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, not just the song title.

label: C
text: song,
analysis: A comma incorrectly detaches the identifying title from song.

label: D
text: song
analysis: No punctuation is needed between the noun and the title that identifies it.

label: A
text: examined
analysis: Incorrect. "Examined" would be a finite past-tense verb taking book titles as its object, followed by the unconnected finite verb shows.

label: B
text: examining
analysis: Correct. "Examining" forms a modifier of macroanalysis, preserving the complete main clause "macroanalysis ... shows."

label: C
text: examines
analysis: Incorrect. "Examines" introduces a second finite present-tense verb without a conjunction to connect it to shows.

label: D
text: had examined
analysis: Incorrect. "Had examined" likewise creates an uncoordinated finite predicate before shows; the past-perfect tense does not solve that structural problem.

label: A
text: nevertheless,
analysis: Nevertheless would signal a contrast absent from the two examples.

label: B
text: likewise,
analysis: Likewise accurately marks the parallel.

label: C
text: hence,
analysis: The first poem does not cause the second poem to take a painting as its subject.

label: D
text: conversely,
analysis: Conversely would reverse a relation that the second example actually repeats.

label: A
text: Nevertheless,
analysis: Nevertheless would oppose the immediately preceding interpretation, though the final claim agrees with it.

label: B
text: For example,
analysis: The final statement is a general conclusion, not a particular example.

label: C
text: Moreover,
analysis: Moreover adds information but does not express the clear consequence as precisely.

label: D
text: As such,
analysis: As such connects the poem's status as a response to its bearing the imprint of change.

label: A
text: The SsWTUF is one of the national union federations represented by ITUC-Africa.

label: A
text: It shows that Mr. Ely had originally been held in high regard by his friends and then details the events that caused their regard for him to subside.
analysis: Incorrect. “It shows that Mr. Ely had originally been held in high regard by his friends and then details the events that caused their regard for him to subside.” — The text never says that anyone's regard subsides and recounts no events that damage his reputation.

label: B
text: It highlights the disparity between Mr. Ely's public and private behavior and then conveys why he labors to obscure his true self from other people.
analysis: Incorrect. “It highlights the disparity between Mr. Ely's public and private behavior and then conveys why he labors to obscure his true self from other people.” — The text describes Mr. Ely's guarded public conduct but neither contrasts it with private behavior nor states a motive to hide a true self.

text: It implies that Mr. Ely's neighbors are more naive in their estimation of him than people in London are and then explains why his neighbors have been so easily misled.
analysis: Incorrect. “It implies that Mr. Ely's neighbors are more naive in their estimation of him than people in London are and then explains why his neighbors have been so easily misled.” — London is mentioned as a place where Milby residents imagine he would impress people, not as a group whose judgment is contrasted with his neighbors' judgment.

label: A
text: It explains a widespread assumption about a phenomenon, describes two studies that are based on that assumption, and explains why the assumption is unfounded.

text: It discusses a particular study of a phenomenon, elaborates on how two other studies have approached this phenomenon in the past, and critiques the first study's approach.

label: C
text: It details the development of a field of scientific inquiry, gives examples of three studies that were important to this development, and speculates on how future studies can develop these ideas.
analysis: Incorrect. “It details the development of a field of scientific inquiry, gives examples of three studies that were important to this development, and speculates on how future studies can develop these ideas.” — The text does not trace the historical development of a field or speculate about future research.

label: D
text: It describes a phenomenon, provides examples of two studies of that phenomenon, and mentions a third study of that phenomenon.
analysis: Correct. “It describes a phenomenon, provides examples of two studies of that phenomenon, and mentions a third study of that phenomenon.” — It accurately follows the passage from the phenomenon to two earlier studies and then to a third study.

label: A
text: The narrator feels optimistic about the future success of a new business.

label: B
text: The narrator recognizes that a particular moment marks a major shift in her life.

text: The narrator has always had a plan for how to handle big moments in her life.

label: D
text: The narrator wants to express her gratitude for the people who have helped her.
analysis: Incorrect. “The narrator wants to express her gratitude for the people who have helped her.” — The paragraph names no helpers and expresses no gratitude; its focus is the narrator's awareness of transition.

label: A
text: Between 2000 and 2019, household incomes rose in Brazil, resulting in households meeting a greater proportion of their fuel needs with high-technology fuels.

text: Beginning in 2000, high-technology fuels became more readily available in Brazil, enabling households of various income levels to shift away from solid fuels.
analysis: Incorrect. “Beginning in 2000, high-technology fuels became more readily available in Brazil, enabling households of various income levels to shift away from solid fuels.” — Emphasizes availability rather than income.

text: Solid fuel use declined in Brazil between 2000 and 2019 because changes in household income during that period made solid fuels more expensive relative to income.
analysis: Incorrect. “Solid fuel use declined in Brazil between 2000 and 2019 because changes in household income during that period made solid fuels more expensive relative to income.” — Claims changing relative price, not the model's mechanism.

text: Household incomes in Brazil rose from 2000 to 2019, which weakened the association between income and household fuel choice.
analysis: Incorrect. “Household incomes in Brazil rose from 2000 to 2019, which weakened the association between income and household fuel choice.” — Says income weakened an association the model relies on.

label: A
text: When foraging along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia, PCFG whales are in closer proximity to major ports and urban populations than ENP whales in the main group are when foraging in Arctic waters.
analysis: Incorrect. “When foraging along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia, PCFG whales are in closer proximity to major ports and urban populations than ENP whales in the main group are when foraging in Arctic waters.” — Proximity to ports and urban populations does not connect smaller body size with access to food resources.

label: B
text: The average body size of PCFG whales observed along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia has remained relatively steady in recent decades, while the average body size of ENP whales in the main group has slightly decreased.
analysis: Incorrect. “The average body size of PCFG whales observed along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia has remained relatively steady in recent decades, while the average body size of ENP whales in the main group has slightly decreased.” — A stable average size shows persistence of the trait, not that resource opportunities caused or favor it.

label: C
text: When present along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia, PCFG whales tend to forage in rocky kelp beds at shallow depths inaccessible to whales as large as those in the ENP main group.
analysis: Correct. “When present along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia, PCFG whales tend to forage in rocky kelp beds at shallow depths inaccessible to whales as large as those in the ENP main group.” — The finding gives smaller whales exclusive access to a foraging habitat, directly linking size to resource opportunity.

label: D
text: Certain crustacean prey species available along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia where PCFG whales tend to forage are not available in the Arctic waters where ENP whales in the main group forage.
analysis: Incorrect. “Certain crustacean prey species available along the coasts of Northern California and British Columbia where PCFG whales tend to forage are not available in the Arctic waters where ENP whales in the main group forage.” — Different prey establishes that the ranges offer different resources, but it does not show why a smaller body is better able to obtain those prey.

label: A

Therefore, A does not fit the prompt, which asks for information not addressed in Text 1.

label: B
text: Did the participants that Cruz and colleagues included in the study share any characteristics or life circumstances?
analysis: Choice B (“Did the participants that Cruz and colleagues included in the study share any characteristics or life circumstances?”): Shared life circumstances are not one of Text 2’s stated methodological concerns. It is not supported by the passage's evidence.

label: C
text: How many Spanish businesspeople did Cruz and colleagues include in the study?
analysis: Choice C (“How many Spanish businesspeople did Cruz and colleagues include in the study?”): The number of participants would address Text 2’s concern about insufficient sample sizes.

label: D
text: Did Cruz and colleagues compare Spanish businesspeople who received the training with a group of successful entrepreneurs who did not receive the training?
analysis: Choice D (“Did Cruz and colleagues compare Spanish businesspeople who received the training with a group of successful entrepreneurs who did not receive the training?”): Text 2 does identify a lack of control groups as a concern, but successful entrepreneurs would not be an appropriate comparable untrained control group for the trainees. Choice C still most directly addresses Text 2’s separate sample-size concern by asking for the missing participant count.

label: A
text: While recommender systems can affect consumer behavior toward suggested products, those effects are not uniform in nature and strength across product categories.
analysis: Choice A (“While recommender systems can affect consumer behavior toward suggested products, those effects are not uniform in nature and strength across product categories.”): Correct: The text reports different effects for utilitarian and hedonic products, so effects vary by category.

label: B
text: By directing customers toward specific product categories on a retailer’s website, recommender systems may limit the variety of items seen by online shoppers.
analysis: Choice B (“By directing customers toward specific product categories on a retailer’s website, recommender systems may limit the variety of items seen by online shoppers.”): The passage gives no evidence that systems limit item variety. It is not supported by the passage's evidence.

label: C
text: By proposing the most useful options to consumers, recommender systems boost the online visibility of utilitarian items that otherwise tend to be overlooked.
analysis: Choice C (“By proposing the most useful options to consumers, recommender systems boost the online visibility of utilitarian items that otherwise tend to be overlooked.”): It does not say systems propose the most useful options or that items are overlooked.

label: D
text: While recommender systems cause consumers to spend more time viewing utilitarian items such as dish detergents, recommender systems’ positive effect on purchase rates is likely limited to hedonic items such as music albums.
analysis: Choice D (“While recommender systems cause consumers to spend more time viewing utilitarian items such as dish detergents, recommender systems’ positive effect on purchase rates is likely…”): It overstates the results by saying the purchase effect is limited to hedonic products. It is not supported by the passage's evidence.

label: A
text: 140 for Class VII.

text: 160 for Class I-IV.

text: radio-collar tracking underestimates the density of cougars.
